["In a case of a 31-week pregnant patient with Takayasu arteritis presenting with shortness of breath and chest pain, the correct diagnosis was chronic obstruction of the right pulmonary artery. The source feedback indicated that while automated tools reported non-specific findings like mild cardiomegaly or lung opacity, the definitive radiographic evidence supporting the answer was a subtle Westermark sign in the right hemithorax, suggestive of chronic vascular obstruction rather than acute embolism or parenchymal disease. This highlights that in Takayasu arteritis, chest X-ray findings may be subtle signs of chronic vascular compromise (such as oligemia or compensatory changes) rather than overt acute pathology, requiring careful interpretation beyond standard automated reports which may miss specific vascular signs.", "In a case involving the diagnosis of pulmonary sequestration, the correct identification relied on recognizing large thin-walled cavities with fluid levels located in the left lower lobe. This specific radiographic presentation supported a diagnosis of intralobar sequestration, distinguishing it from other conditions like bronchiectasis, cystic fibrosis, or pneumonia which present with different cavity characteristics or distributions. It is noted that automated chest X-ray classification tools may fail to identify these specific findings (returning no strong findings), and report generators may incorrectly describe the lungs as clear; therefore, reliance on direct visual interpretation of the cavity location (left lower lobe) and morphology (thin-walled, fluid levels) is critical for accurate diagnosis when tool outputs are non-contributory or contradictory."]
